# Learning a language from your own materials

A textbook is written for everybody, which means it is written for nobody in particular. The texts you read on your own are different: you chose them, so you already care about what they say.

## Why your own texts work better

When the topic is familiar, the unknown words are surrounded by known ones. You guess, and most of the time your guess is close enough. That is how vocabulary grows outside a classroom.

- Read something you would read in your own language anyway.
- Keep the text short enough to finish in one sitting.
- Write down only the words that appear more than once.
- Say the new sentences out loud before you close the file.

## A simple weekly plan

Monday and Tuesday are for reading. Wednesday is for speaking about what you read, even if there is nobody to listen: describing a text to an empty room is still practice. Thursday is for mistakes — the ones you collected during the week, sorted and repeated. Friday is for something easy and pleasant, because a habit that hurts every day does not survive the month.

## What to expect

Progress in a language is not a straight line. There are weeks when nothing seems to move, and then a morning when a sentence you never studied simply makes sense. The weeks of apparent silence are the ones doing the work.
